Making a dummy API call at application startup specifically to populate the prompt cache with the system prompt and knowledge base — important for latency-sensitive applications where the first real user request must not pay the full input processing cost
A technique to improve Claude's accuracy over time
Increasing the cache TTL to avoid cache expiration
qs.ex: Cache warming ensures the first user request is fast. Without warming, the first request after a cold start pays full input processing cost (high latency). A startup call with cache_control markers populates the cache so all subsequent user requests hit the cached prefix.

qs.q: In a production multi-agent system, what is the MOST effective pattern for preventing runaway costs?
opts: Set a hard token limit per subagent and terminate immediately when reached

Implement a hierarchical budget system: total session budget at orchestrator level, per-agent budgets as allocations — with early-warning alerts and graceful degradation when budgets are near-exhausted
Monitor costs post-hoc and alert the finance team if a session exceeds thresholds
Use only Haiku models for all subagents to minimize per-call cost
qs.ex: Hierarchical budgeting is production-grade: the orchestrator allocates a per-session budget and distributes sub-budgets to each agent. Early warnings allow graceful degradation before hitting hard limits.

qs.q: What is the key design consideration when implementing a 'trust hierarchy' between a coordinator agent and its subagents?
opts: All agents should share the same API key to simplify credential management
Subagents should be able to override coordinator decisions when they have higher confidence
Subagents should validate that instructions come from trusted sources and reject or escalate instructions that exceed their defined permission boundaries
Each subagent should have full visibility into all other agents' contexts for coordination
qs.ex: Trust hierarchies define what each agent may do and who may instruct it. Subagents should validate instruction sources and refuse instructions that exceed their authorization scope.

qs.q: A production agentic system needs to handle failures where a subagent's output is silently wrong (no exception thrown, but incorrect result). What architecture pattern addresses this?
opts: Increase the number of retries for each subagent call
Add a validator agent that independently verifies key subagent outputs against expected schemas and business-logic invariants
Use a more capable model for all subagents to reduce error rate
Log all subagent outputs and review them weekly
qs.ex: Silent failures are the hardest to detect. A dedicated validator agent checking outputs against schemas and invariants (not just format, but semantic correctness) catches these before they propagate downstream.

qs.q: When building a production RAG system with Claude, what is the MOST important failure mode to design against?
opts: Claude generating responses that are too long
The retrieval step returning no results — causing Claude to fall back to training-time knowledge without clear indication to the user
API rate limits slowing retrieval throughput
PDF parsing errors losing document content

qs.q: What distinguishes 'indirect prompt injection' from direct prompt injection attacks?
opts: It only affects multimodal inputs, not text-based systems
Adversarial instructions are embedded in documents or web pages that Claude reads during tool use — potentially overriding system prompt instructions without any direct user input
It requires the attacker to have API access to the system
It only occurs with temperature > 0.5
qs.ex: Indirect prompt injection happens when Claude reads external content (a web page, database record) that contains embedded adversarial instructions. The attacker never touches the API.

qs.q: What is a 'golden test set' and why is it essential for production Claude deployments?
opts: A collection of the best prompts Claude has ever generated
A curated set of representative inputs with known-correct outputs used to benchmark quality, detect regressions, and make upgrade decisions
A gold-standard dataset Anthropic provides to partners
A list of prompts that Claude always answers correctly, used to set SLA expectations
qs.ex: A golden test set is your quality baseline. It captures representative real-world inputs with expected outputs. Run it on every model update, prompt change, or deployment change to catch regressions before users do.

qs.q: Your team wants to upgrade to a new Claude model version. What is the correct migration process?
opts: Update the model name string in production immediately — newer versions are always better
Run the upgrade only on weekends when traffic is low
Evaluate the new model on your golden test set, deploy to a small percentage of traffic (canary), monitor key metrics, then progressively roll out after validating quality and performance
Upgrade a single endpoint first and ask users to report problems
qs.ex: Progressive rollout with evaluation is the production-safe approach. Golden test set evaluation catches regressions; canary deployment limits blast radius; progressive rollout gives confidence before full migration.

qs.q: In a regulated industry (healthcare, finance), what governance artifact is MOST important for an AI deployment?
opts: A version-controlled log of all system prompt changes with deployment dates and approvers
Marketing materials explaining Claude's capabilities to stakeholders
A record of API costs by month
A comparison of Claude versus competing models
qs.ex: In regulated industries, auditability is paramount. Version-controlled prompt histories with change management (who approved what change, when, what was the justification) are essential for regulatory examination.

qs.q: What is 'output monitoring' in a production Claude deployment and why is it essential?
opts: Monitoring the length of Claude's responses to control costs
Systematic logging and analysis of Claude's outputs to detect quality degradation, policy violations, hallucinations, or adversarial outputs — enabling rapid detection and response
Monitoring the Claude API dashboard for uptime
Reviewing Claude's system prompt for outdated instructions monthly
qs.ex: Output monitoring is your production safety net. It detects when Claude drifts from expected behavior — due to model changes, prompt injection, or adversarial inputs — before systematic harm accumulates.

qs.q: When managing shared system prompts across 100 engineers and multiple use cases, what is the MOST scalable approach?
opts: Each engineer maintains their own copy of the system prompt
Hardcode the system prompt in the application source code
Store system prompts in a versioned configuration store, with CI/CD pipelines deploying prompt changes through test, staging, and production — treating prompts as first-class code artifacts
Use a shared Google Doc that engineers edit collaboratively
qs.ex: Treating prompts as code is the production-grade approach. Version control, PR reviews, automated golden-set testing, and staged deployment give the same quality guarantees as application code.

qs.q: A multi-agent pipeline has a 45-second p95 latency. The bottleneck is three sequential tool calls, each waiting on the previous. What is the recommended optimization?
opts: Use a larger model — more capable models run tool calls faster
Reduce the max_tokens limit to make Claude respond more quickly
Refactor the pipeline so independent tool calls execute in parallel, waiting only on genuine data dependencies
Cache all tool responses permanently to avoid repeated calls

qs.q: Context window usage is 85% at the start of each session due to a large system prompt and document context. How do you reduce this?
opts: Switch to a model with a larger context window as a permanent solution
Compress the system prompt to fewer than 50 words
Implement hierarchical context: store reference material externally, load only relevant sections dynamically based on the current task
Remove tool definitions to free up context space
qs.ex: Dynamic context loading is the scalable solution. Instead of loading everything upfront, use search and retrieval to pull in only the context relevant to the current step.

qs.q: You want to implement caching for Claude API responses to reduce costs. What is the key risk?
opts: Cached responses use more memory than API calls
Cached responses may be served for similar-but-not-identical queries, returning incorrect answers — stale cache is particularly dangerous when underlying data changes
API response caching is not permitted by Anthropic's terms of service
Caching always degrades response quality
qs.ex: Caching Claude responses requires careful cache key design and invalidation. Overly broad keys serve wrong answers; stale caches serve outdated answers. Cache only truly stable, deterministic query-response pairs.

qs.q: Which technique BEST reduces latency for a deployment where the first user query is always one of 10 known question types?
opts: Pre-generate responses for all 10 question types at startup and serve them as static strings
Use a classifier (a faster model or traditional ML) to identify the question type and route to a specialized prompt tailored for that type
Implement extended thinking for all queries to improve first-response quality
Increase the API timeout threshold
qs.ex: Classification-based routing is a powerful optimization. A cheap, fast classifier identifies the question type; the application routes to the optimized prompt, context, and model tier for that type.

qs.q: What is 'speculative execution' in the context of multi-step Claude pipelines?
opts: Running the pipeline twice to verify results are identical
Starting downstream pipeline steps in parallel before upstream steps complete, using predicted outputs — then correcting when the actual outputs arrive
Using Claude to speculate about future user requests
Running expensive steps only when the simple path fails
qs.ex: Speculative execution pre-starts downstream steps with predicted inputs. If the prediction is correct, you save the latency of waiting. Effective when upstream outputs are predictable and downstream steps take significant time.

qs.q: You are designing a Claude-powered system that processes sensitive financial data. Which data handling approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Send all raw financial data to Claude in full for comprehensive analysis
Implement data minimization — anonymize PII, aggregate sensitive fields, and send only the minimum data necessary for the task
Use client-side encryption so Anthropic cannot read the data
Store all data in Claude's context between sessions for continuity
qs.ex: Data minimization reduces exposure: anonymize PII (replace names with IDs), aggregate where exact values aren't needed, and never send more than the task requires. Claude processes what it receives — reduce data, reduce risk.

qs.q: A production system needs Claude to handle 10,000 customer queries per day with consistent quality. What architecture best supports this at scale?
opts: A single production server running one Claude session for all queries
A serverless architecture with stateless request handlers, model version pinning, prompt versioning, output monitoring, and rate limit handling with retry queues
A dedicated on-premise Claude deployment
A human review team that validates all Claude outputs before delivery
qs.ex: Stateless, serverless architecture scales horizontally. Model pinning ensures consistent quality. Prompt versioning enables safe updates. Output monitoring detects quality drift. Retry queues handle transient API failures gracefully.

qs.q: When building a multi-tenant Claude deployment, what is the MOST important security consideration?
opts: Using separate API keys for each customer
Ensuring one customer's context (system prompt, conversation history, data) can never bleed into another customer's session through shared state or caching
Using different Claude models for different customer tiers
Monitoring total token usage per customer for billing purposes
qs.ex: Tenant isolation is the critical security property. Shared state — whether from cache, session state, or database — that leaks from one tenant to another is a serious security incident.

qs.q: What evaluation framework is BEST suited for measuring whether a Claude-powered code review system improves over time?
opts: Measure only API latency and cost — quality is subjective
Track average user star ratings of Claude's code review comments
Build a labeled dataset of code samples with expert-judged review quality scores, then measure Claude's performance against this dataset before and after any system change
Count the number of code reviews Claude completes per day
qs.ex: Labeled evaluation data with expert ground truth is the foundation of systematic quality measurement. It enables A/B testing between prompt versions, model upgrades, and configuration changes — turning opinion into data.

qs.q: A deployed Claude system begins producing inconsistent answers to the same question — sometimes contradicting previous responses. What is the MOST likely root cause?
opts: Claude's API has a bug that introduces random noise
The system prompt is not deterministic — different tool results, variable context loading, or non-zero temperature cause natural variation
The model has been retrained since deployment without notification
The user is asking questions incorrectly
qs.ex: Response variation stems from non-determinism: temperature > 0, variable context (different tool results, different amounts of history), or non-stable prompts. Use temperature=0, stable context loading, and pin to a specific model version.

qs.q: You need to ensure that a Claude-powered legal document system never outputs content that contradicts the jurisdiction's current statutes. What architecture provides the STRONGEST guarantee?
opts: Use the most capable Claude model available — higher capability means fewer errors
Include a note in the system prompt saying 'always follow current law'
Implement a post-generation validation layer that checks Claude's output against a verified statutory database and flags or blocks non-compliant content before it reaches users
Use temperature=0 to ensure deterministic legal interpretations
qs.ex: Post-generation validation against an authoritative external source is the strongest architecture. It doesn't trust Claude to self-regulate; it independently checks every output against ground truth before delivery.

qs.q: A partner solution uses a long stable policy block on every request. Which cost-and-latency lever matches Architect Professional guidance?
opts: Disable all caching forever
Prompt caching on the repeated prefix, then keep the changing user turn uncached
Print the policy on paper
Use only image inputs
qs.ex: Professional domain 2 covers model tiers, prompting, and caching. Shared prefixes are the classic cache win.

qs.q: You must expose an internal CRM to Claude without dumping the entire schema into every prompt. What integration shape is usually right?
opts: Paste the full database into the system prompt
MCP or scoped tools with progressive discovery — Claude fetches only the records the task needs
Email the database to Anthropic support
One giant resource that returns every table
qs.ex: Integration is the heaviest CCAR-P domain. Scoped tools and MCP beat a monolithic dump (capability bloat).

qs.q: A client asks you to skip discovery and jump straight to an autonomous agent. What should you produce first?
opts: A production cutover date only
Discovery outputs: goals, constraints, data sensitivity, success metrics, and whether a workflow or an agent is even the right pattern
A Credly badge screenshot
An exam voucher
qs.ex: Professional domain 6 is lifecycle and stakeholders. Pattern choice belongs in discovery, not after go-live.

qs.q: Ten engineers use Claude Code on the same monorepo with conflicting styles. What is the enablement fix?
opts: Each person invents private rules
Shared CLAUDE.md, agreed Skills/hooks, and a short team playbook so sessions behave the same
Ban Claude Code
Only use Associate chat
qs.ex: Domain 7 is team configuration of Claude Code — shared instructions, not one-off personal chats.

qs.q: A client wants to build an AI system that automatically files support tickets without any human review. What is the correct architect response?
opts: Build exactly what they asked for — client knows best
Build it, but add a low-confidence threshold that routes unsure cases to humans
Recommend against full automation initially; propose a human-in-the-loop model that earns trust, then expands autonomy as accuracy is validated over time
Refuse to build any autonomous system
qs.ex: Earning autonomy is the professional pattern. Full automation from day one without a trust track record is high risk. Start HITL, establish a quality baseline, expand automation only where the data supports it.

qs.q: When is a single-agent architecture preferable to multi-agent?
opts: Always — coordination overhead is never worth it
When the task is well-defined, fits within a single context window, and doesn't benefit from parallel execution or domain specialization
When you have fewer than 10 tools available
When the task is expected to take less than 30 seconds
qs.ex: Multi-agent adds coordination complexity. Use it only when the payoff — parallelism or domain specialization — outweighs the coordination cost. For simple tasks that fit one context, a single focused agent is faster and easier to debug.

qs.q: What is the 'minimal footprint' principle for agentic system design?
opts: Use the cheapest possible models to minimize API costs
Design agents to request only necessary permissions, store only necessary data, and prefer reversible actions — minimizing risk and blast radius of errors
Limit each agent to a maximum of 5 tool calls per session
Prefer no-code solutions over code-based automation
qs.ex: Minimal footprint is a safety design principle: request only needed permissions (least privilege), store only needed data (data minimization), prefer reversible over irreversible actions (blast radius reduction). Errors in minimal-footprint agents have smaller consequences.

qs.q: What architecture decision record (ADR) should you produce before building a multi-agent system for a regulated financial client?
opts: A cost estimate only
A document covering: business problem, candidate patterns evaluated, chosen pattern, key trade-offs, data sensitivity classification, compliance implications, and rollback plan
A diagram of agent boxes with arrows
A Gantt chart of the implementation timeline
qs.ex: An ADR for regulated environments must capture the decision rationale, alternatives considered, trade-offs accepted, and compliance implications. It becomes an audit artifact demonstrating due diligence.

qs.q: A client asks you to compare a workflow versus an agent for their document classification use case. The documents have exactly 5 possible categories and a clear decision tree. Which do you recommend?
opts: Agent — it is more capable
Workflow — the task is fully deterministic and doesn't require dynamic decision-making
Agent — workflows can't classify documents
Workflow — but only if cost is the primary concern
qs.ex: A deterministic decision tree maps directly to a workflow: extract features, apply rules, assign category. An agent's dynamic decision-making adds complexity without benefit. Always prefer the simpler solution when it's sufficient.

qs.q: What is the correct model selection strategy for a system that processes requests ranging from simple FAQ lookups to complex multi-document legal analysis?
opts: Use the most capable model for all requests to ensure consistent quality
Implement a routing layer: classify each request by complexity and route to the appropriate model tier (Haiku for FAQ, Sonnet for standard, Opus for complex)
Use the cheapest model by default and upgrade only when requests fail
Let users choose their preferred model
qs.ex: Complexity-based routing optimizes the cost-quality trade-off at every request. A cheap, fast classifier identifies request complexity; each tier gets the model appropriate for its needs. This is the production-grade approach.

qs.q: Extended thinking is MOST beneficial for which type of task?
opts: Simple factual lookups where speed matters
Multi-step mathematical proofs or complex reasoning tasks where working through intermediate steps correctly is required for a valid final answer
Creative writing where variety is desired
Summarization of short documents
qs.ex: Extended thinking provides dedicated internal reasoning space. It pays off on tasks where intermediate steps matter — math, logic, multi-constraint problem solving. For simple lookups or creative tasks, the latency cost isn't justified.

qs.q: You are building a production system where the same 40,000-token knowledge base is used in every request. What optimization applies?
opts: Summarize the knowledge base to 4,000 tokens once and use the summary
Use prompt caching to cache the knowledge base prefix — after the first call, cached tokens cost ~90% less and load faster
Split the knowledge base across multiple separate API calls
Store the knowledge base in Claude's memory between sessions
qs.ex: Prompt caching is the exact optimization for this use case. A large, stable prefix (knowledge base + system prompt) is cached after the first request. Subsequent requests reuse the cache, dramatically reducing cost and latency.

qs.q: What is 'token budget management' in a production agentic system?
opts: Counting output tokens to control response length
Proactively tracking total token consumption across the entire session and agent chain, with mechanisms to prevent runaway usage from exhausting budgets or triggering unexpected costs
Monitoring monthly API costs and sending alerts
Setting max_tokens limits on individual API calls
qs.ex: Budget management is session-level and cross-agent. Track total consumption (input + output + cached), set per-agent budgets, implement early warnings, and define graceful degradation when budgets near exhaustion.

qs.q: A RAG system returns retrieval results that are sometimes relevant and sometimes not. What is the most reliable way to prevent Claude from using irrelevant retrieved content?
opts: Include a relevance score in the retrieved chunks and instruct Claude to ignore chunks below a threshold
Trust Claude to filter relevant from irrelevant content automatically
Use only BM25 retrieval to ensure precision
Increase the number of retrieved chunks to improve coverage
qs.ex: Relevance scoring + threshold instruction is the correct pattern. The retrieval system scores chunks; Claude receives the score and an explicit instruction to skip low-scoring chunks. This combines retrieval quality with language model judgment.

qs.q: What is the difference between 'retrieval-augmented generation' (RAG) and 'fine-tuning' for adding domain knowledge to Claude?
opts: RAG and fine-tuning are two names for the same process
RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and includes them in context — knowledge stays external and current; fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights — knowledge is static after training
RAG is more expensive than fine-tuning
Fine-tuning produces better results for all use cases
qs.ex: RAG: external knowledge retrieved at query time — always current, no training cost, transparent. Fine-tuning: knowledge baked into weights — fast at inference, but static after training and opaque. For most production cases, RAG is preferred for its updatability.

qs.q: When building an integration between Claude and a relational database, what is the security-correct approach for passing SQL queries?
opts: Let Claude generate raw SQL and execute it directly against the database
Use parameterized queries or a structured tool that converts Claude's intent into safe database operations — never execute Claude-generated SQL directly
Store Claude's SQL in a file and have a DBA review it before execution
Use a read-only database user so even malicious SQL can't cause damage
qs.ex: Direct execution of LLM-generated SQL is a SQL injection risk. Use parameterized queries or a structured interface where Claude specifies intent (filter by X, sort by Y) and your code converts it to a safe parameterized query.

qs.q: Your vector database has 10 million documents. A user query retrieves the top-20 semantically similar chunks. What additional filtering step improves answer accuracy?
opts: Return all 10 million documents and let Claude pick the best ones
Apply a metadata filter before semantic search (e.g., restrict to documents matching the user's department or date range) to reduce the search space and improve precision
Use the BM25 algorithm instead of vector similarity
Always retrieve exactly 10 chunks regardless of similarity scores
qs.ex: Metadata pre-filtering is a high-impact retrieval optimization. Filtering by known user attributes (department, time range, document type) before vector search dramatically improves precision by eliminating out-of-scope documents.

qs.q: What does 'flaky evaluation' mean in the context of LLM testing?
opts: An evaluation that takes too long to run
An evaluation that produces different pass/fail results for the same prompt and model due to non-determinism — usually from temperature > 0 or variable context
An evaluation with insufficient test cases
An evaluation that runs on the wrong model
qs.ex: Flaky evals produce unreliable signals. Fix by: temperature=0 (or set a very low temperature), pinning to a specific model version, using a fixed random seed, and ensuring context is consistent. Without stable evals, you can't reliably measure improvement.

qs.q: What is LLM-as-judge evaluation and when is it appropriate?
opts: Using Claude to write your evaluation test cases before running them
Using a Claude instance to score another Claude instance's outputs on dimensions like relevance, accuracy, and coherence — appropriate when ground truth is hard to define but quality can be judged
Using Claude to judge whether evaluation results justify a model upgrade
A technique where multiple models vote on the best output
qs.ex: LLM-as-judge works well for subjective quality dimensions (coherence, helpfulness, relevance) where a fixed rubric is hard to write. Use a capable model as judge, provide clear scoring criteria, and validate the judge's calibration against human scores.

qs.q: A production system has three quality metrics: accuracy, latency, and cost. A new prompt change improves accuracy by 5% but increases latency by 30% and cost by 20%. What is the correct decision process?
opts: Always accept quality improvements regardless of cost
Reject the change — any latency increase is unacceptable
Evaluate the trade-off against business requirements: is 5% accuracy worth 30% latency and 20% cost? Different use cases have different answer
Accept only if your SLA allows 30% more latency
qs.ex: Trade-off decisions require business context. A medical diagnosis system might accept 30% latency for 5% accuracy; a real-time chat system cannot. Define acceptable trade-off ranges before evaluating changes.

qs.q: What is the correct approach for evaluating a Claude system that generates creative marketing copy?
opts: Reject LLM-based systems for creative use cases — they cannot be evaluated objectively
Use automated BLEU/ROUGE scores to measure copy quality
Define a structured rubric with human judges: on-brand score, clarity, call-to-action strength, grammar. Run a sample weekly and track trend lines
Accept all outputs since quality is purely subjective
qs.ex: Creative quality requires a defined rubric. Even subjective tasks can be made measurable with a structured rubric and human judges. Track trend lines over time to detect quality drift — this is what makes creative AI systems improvable.

qs.q: What is a 'red team' exercise for a Claude deployment and why is it valuable?
opts: A team that manages cost reduction for Claude API usage
A structured adversarial testing exercise where a team attempts to find failure modes, policy violations, and exploits before the system goes live
A team that reviews Claude's system prompt for quality
A regulatory audit of AI usage in the organization
qs.ex: Red teaming is pre-production adversarial testing. By simulating attacks, misuse patterns, and edge cases before go-live, you discover failure modes that standard testing misses. Particularly important for customer-facing systems.

qs.q: What is the 'principle of least privilege' applied to Claude tool access?
opts: Give Claude the minimum number of tools necessary for the task — never expose tools it won't need
Always give Claude read-only tools only
Restrict Claude to a maximum of 5 tools per session
Rotate which tools Claude has access to on each request
qs.ex: Least privilege for tools: expose only the tools needed for the current task. A document summarization agent doesn't need file deletion tools. Minimal tool exposure reduces the blast radius of misuse or errors.

qs.q: How should you handle PII in a Claude-powered customer service system?
opts: Pass all customer data to Claude for full context — more context is always better

Implement data minimization: pass only the fields Claude needs for the specific task, tokenize or redact sensitive fields (SSNs, credit card numbers), and never log Claude's input or output when it contains raw PII
Store all customer PII in Claude's context for the entire session for consistency
Encrypt all data before sending to Claude
qs.ex: Data minimization is the correct PII handling pattern. Send only needed fields, redact sensitive ones (tokenize SSNs), and implement appropriate log retention policies. This limits exposure and simplifies compliance.

qs.q: A system prompt version was deployed that contained a subtle error causing Claude to occasionally recommend competitor products. How should this be handled from a governance perspective?
opts: Fix the system prompt immediately and move on

Fix the prompt, version the change in your system prompt registry, document what went wrong, calculate the scope of affected users, notify affected users if required, and add a test to the golden set that would have caught this error
Delete all logs of the incident
Fix the prompt without documenting the incident to avoid regulatory scrutiny
qs.ex: Incident response for AI governance: fix, document, scope, notify, improve. The golden set update is critical — every production incident should produce a test case that prevents the same failure.

qs.q: When presenting an AI system's quality metrics to non-technical executives, what is the most effective communication format?
opts: Detailed F1 scores, precision, recall, and BLEU scores
High-level business outcomes: error rate reduction, cost savings, user satisfaction trend, and a clear statement of what the system will and won't do
Technical architecture diagrams
A comparison of Claude vs. GPT-4 benchmark scores
qs.ex: Executive communication translates technical metrics to business outcomes. 'Our error rate dropped from 8% to 2%, saving 3 FTE hours per day' is more actionable than 'our F1 improved from 0.72 to 0.89'.

qs.q: A client asks you to guarantee 99.9% accuracy for a Claude-powered document review system. How do you respond?
opts: Accept the guarantee — Claude is very accurate
Guarantee 99% instead as a compromise

Explain that LLMs are probabilistic systems; propose a measurable SLA based on your evaluation data (e.g., 'Error rate on our test set is 2.3%') and a monitoring plan to detect deviation, rather than an absolute accuracy guarantee
Reject the project — AI systems can't have accuracy SLAs
qs.ex: Probabilistic systems need probabilistic SLAs. Replace absolute guarantees with measured baselines + monitoring + alert thresholds. This is honest, defensible, and gives the client actionable expectations.

qs.q: What is the correct order of activities in a responsible AI deployment lifecycle?
opts: Build → Test → Deploy → Monitor
Discover → Architect → Build → Evaluate → Deploy → Monitor → Iterate
Deploy → Evaluate → Fix
Build → Deploy → Monitor → Discover problems
qs.ex: The responsible AI lifecycle starts with discovery (understand the problem, data, risk), then architecture (choose the right pattern), build, evaluate against criteria, deploy with monitoring, and iterate based on signals. Skipping discovery causes the wrong thing to be built.

qs.q: A production Claude system's quality has degraded over three weeks. Who should be notified, and in what order?
opts: No one — fix it quietly
The product team first (to understand user impact), then engineering (to diagnose), then the client relationship owner (to communicate proactively), then affected users if required by SLA
Only the engineering team — it's a technical problem
All stakeholders simultaneously via mass email
qs.ex: Structured escalation: understand impact first, then diagnose, then communicate outward. Proactive client communication before they notice is relationship-preserving. User notification follows if SLA or contractual obligations require it.

qs.q: How do you measure the ROI of Claude Code adoption in a development team?
opts: Count the number of times Claude Code is used per day
Track: time-to-PR (does it decrease?), revert rate (does code quality hold?), test coverage trends, and developer satisfaction scores — compare before and after adoption
Only measure cost reduction from fewer developer hours
Survey developers on whether they 'feel more productive'
qs.ex: ROI measurement for developer tools should track outcomes: PR velocity, code quality (revert rate, defect density), and developer satisfaction. Usage metrics alone don't prove value — outcome metrics do.

qs.q: A team member complains that Claude Code is making them too dependent on AI and they're not learning. What is the architect's recommended response?
opts: Disable Claude Code for that team member
Encourage using Claude Code in 'teach me' mode — asking Claude to explain its decisions — and reserving complex problem-solving sessions where the developer works alone first
Force the team member to use Claude Code anyway
Accept reduced Claude Code usage as a trade-off for skill development
qs.ex: Productive AI use is about augmentation, not replacement. Developers who ask Claude to explain its reasoning learn more than those who accept outputs blindly. Structured practices (explain mode, personal sessions without AI) maintain and develop skills.

qs.q: What is the recommended team practice for evolving CLAUDE.md over time?
opts: Never change CLAUDE.md once it is written
Treat CLAUDE.md changes as code changes: propose via PR, review with the team, test with a sample task before merging, and keep a changelog of what changed and why
Allow any team member to edit CLAUDE.md directly without review
Update CLAUDE.md quarterly in a batch process
qs.ex: CLAUDE.md-as-code means the same process as code: PR, review, test, merge, changelog. This prevents unilateral changes that break other team members' workflows and maintains a history of why rules were added.

qs.q: What is 'agent orchestration overhead' and how do you minimize it?
opts: The API cost of running multiple agent calls — minimize by using fewer agents
The coordination cost (context passing, state management, latency) of multi-agent systems — minimize by only splitting into agents when the benefit (parallelism/specialization) exceeds this overhead
The time it takes to set up agent configurations — minimize by using templates
The token cost of agent system prompts — minimize by writing short prompts
qs.ex: Orchestration overhead is real: passing context, managing state, and coordinating agents adds latency and complexity. The discipline is: only use multi-agent when the parallel speedup or specialization benefit clearly exceeds this overhead.

qs.q: A production system's context window is consistently 90% full by turn 3 of a conversation. What is the long-term architectural fix?
opts: Switch to a model with a larger context window — this always solves the problem

Implement conversation state management: summarize completed topics, maintain a rolling working memory of recent turns and key facts, and retrieve relevant history on demand rather than keeping everything in context
Ask users to start new conversations more frequently
Reduce the system prompt size to 50 words
qs.ex: Conversation state management is the architectural solution. Summarize completed threads, keep only recent context active, retrieve relevant history as needed. This enables conversations of arbitrary length without context exhaustion.

qs.q: What is 'regression testing' in the context of a Claude deployment, and what triggers it?
opts: Testing that Claude hasn't gotten worse over time — triggered manually whenever a team member notices a problem
Systematically running the golden test set against any system change (prompt edit, model upgrade, tool change) to detect quality decreases before the change reaches production
Testing for regulatory compliance — triggered by audits
Running the same request 10 times to check consistency — triggered before every deployment
qs.ex: Regression testing is automated quality protection. Every change (prompt, model, configuration) triggers a golden set run before deployment. This catches quality decreases before users experience them — the same principle as unit testing in software development.

qs.q: What is a 'circuit breaker' pattern in a production Claude deployment?
opts: A hardware safety mechanism for data center power

An automated mechanism that detects when a Claude system is producing problematic outputs at scale (quality below threshold, policy violations above threshold) and automatically stops or limits the system until human review
A system prompt that prevents Claude from discussing competitors
A monitoring dashboard that alerts when API costs exceed budget
qs.ex: Circuit breakers provide automated protection at scale. When monitoring detects systematic failures (policy violations, quality drops), the circuit breaker automatically reduces traffic or stops the system — preventing widespread harm before human review.

qs.q: When building a Claude integration for real-time customer support, what is the most important SLA consideration?
opts: Cost per conversation
P99 response latency — most users are satisfied if average latency is acceptable, but the worst 1% of responses determine whether the system 'feels slow'
Average latency — the mean is most representative
Total daily API cost
qs.ex: P99 latency (worst-case experience) often matters more than average. Users who occasionally wait 30 seconds remember it even if the average is 2 seconds. Design for worst-case latency, not just average case.

qs.q: What is 'AI readiness assessment' and when should you perform it?
opts: A test of whether Claude's API is operational — run hourly
An evaluation of the client organization's data quality, process maturity, change management capability, and AI governance before committing to a production deployment — done during discovery
A benchmark of Claude vs. competitors — run at contract signing
An annual review of the deployment's ROI
qs.ex: AI readiness assessment in discovery determines whether the organization is prepared for AI adoption — not just technically, but culturally and operationally. Poor data quality, change resistance, or absent governance are as likely to cause failure as technical issues.

qs.q: A client's business problem is: 'We receive 500 customer emails per day and want to reduce the time our support team spends reading them.' What is the FIRST architectural question you must answer?
opts: Which Claude model costs least
What percentage of emails can be fully automated vs. which require human judgment — this determines whether you build an automation, an assistant, or a triage tool
How many tokens does a typical email contain
Whether the client uses Gmail or Outlook
qs.ex: Automation percentage is the key design fork. If 80% of emails are standard requests (order status, FAQ) → full automation with escalation. If 80% require judgment → an assistant that drafts for human review. Getting this wrong means building the wrong system.

qs.q: When selecting between Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus for a production system, which criterion is MOST important?
opts: Always choose the newest model
Match the model to the task complexity and latency/cost budget: Haiku for simple/fast/cheap, Sonnet for balanced, Opus for maximum capability on complex tasks
Choose based on company preference
Use Opus for all production work to ensure quality
qs.ex: Model selection is a cost-quality-latency triangle. Haiku handles classification/routing/short generation efficiently. Sonnet handles most production tasks. Opus is for tasks requiring the deepest reasoning where cost and latency are acceptable.

qs.q: A Claude solution must handle ambiguous business requirements from a client who says 'make it intelligent'. What is the architect's correct response?
opts: Build the most comprehensive system possible
Ask: what specific decisions do you want the system to make, what inputs does it have, and how will you measure whether 'intelligent' is achieved — then scope to those specific decisions
Interpret 'intelligent' as autonomous agent and build accordingly
Use the largest available model to maximize intelligence
qs.ex: 'Intelligent' is not a requirement — it's a desired outcome. Discovery uncovers the specific decisions the system must make, the inputs available, the expected quality bar, and the measurement criteria. This is what translates into an architecturally sound scoping.

qs.q: Which reference architecture is correct for a document Q&A system where the knowledge base changes weekly?
opts: Fine-tune Claude on the document set monthly
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): index documents in a vector store, retrieve relevant chunks at query time — knowledge updates are handled by re-indexing, not retraining
Load all documents into Claude's context on every query
Use a rule-based system for document search and Claude only for final answer generation
qs.ex: RAG is the canonical architecture for updatable knowledge bases. Re-indexing (chunking and embedding) is far cheaper and faster than retraining. Claude receives relevant chunks via context and synthesizes an answer from the retrieved evidence.

qs.q: What is a 'context strategy' in Claude solution design, and why does it matter?
opts: The strategy for getting Claude to follow instructions — more context always means better results

The plan for what information goes into Claude's context window, in what format, and in what order — it determines whether Claude has the right information at the right time without wasting tokens or degrading quality
The number of conversation turns allowed before resetting
The model's internal memory mechanism
qs.ex: Context strategy is an architectural decision: what knowledge does Claude need, how is it structured (system prompt vs. retrieved chunks vs. conversation history), how much fits in the budget, and what gets dropped when the budget fills. Poor context strategy is a top cause of production quality failures.

qs.q: A client wants a Claude-powered coding assistant that suggests the next function to write. What is the minimum viable input the system must provide to Claude?
opts: The entire codebase in context
The current file, the function signature being worked on, relevant imported types/interfaces, and any related test files — enough context to understand the design contract without the whole codebase
Just the current function signature
The error message from the last compile
qs.ex: Minimum viable context for code suggestion: current file (local structure), relevant signatures (interface contract), and related tests (behavioral spec). The entire codebase is usually too large and contains too much irrelevant noise.

qs.q: When is fine-tuning a better choice than RAG for a production Claude deployment?
opts: When you have more than 1,000 documents
When the target behavior is a style, format, or tone that must be deeply consistent across all outputs — and that style cannot be reliably produced by prompting alone
Fine-tuning is always better for production
When the knowledge base changes frequently
qs.ex: Fine-tuning encodes style and behavioral patterns into the model weights. It's appropriate for: consistent tone/voice, specialized output formats, or domain vocabulary that is hard to prompt into. For factual knowledge that changes, RAG is better because it's updatable.

qs.q: A Claude system designed as a PoC uses synchronous API calls with 30-second timeouts. What must change for enterprise production?
opts: Nothing — PoC architecture scales directly

Replace synchronous calls with an async job queue (SQS/Pub-Sub) for long tasks, add streaming for interactive responses, implement retry logic with exponential backoff, and set appropriate timeout policies per use case
Increase timeout to 5 minutes
Use a different API provider with guaranteed response times
qs.ex: PoC-to-production transformation for latency: async queues for long tasks (LLM inference can take 30s+ for complex prompts), streaming for UX (show tokens as they arrive), retry with backoff (transient failures), and per-SLA timeout policies.

qs.q: How do you calculate the total cost of a Claude API call in production for budgeting purposes?
opts: output_tokens × output_price
(input_tokens × input_price) + (output_tokens × output_price) — and for cached calls: (cache_read_tokens × cache_read_price) + (new_input_tokens × input_price) + (output_tokens × output_price)
Flat rate per API call
input_tokens only — output is always free
qs.ex: Total cost = input cost + output cost (+ cache read cost if using prompt caching). Both sides matter: a system prompt with 10,000 tokens on every call has significant input cost even for short outputs. Budget modeling must account for both sides.

qs.q: What is 'integration pattern selection' in enterprise Claude deployment, and what are the key patterns?
opts: Choosing between REST and GraphQL for the API

Deciding how Claude fits into the broader enterprise system: synchronous request-response (chatbot), async batch (document processing), event-driven (triggered by system events), or embedded (Claude call inside a larger workflow)
Selecting the authentication method
Choosing between Claude and other AI providers
qs.ex: Integration pattern determines how Claude fits the enterprise's event model. Chatbot = sync R/R. Document processing = async batch. Compliance monitoring = event-driven. Report generation = embedded in a workflow. Pattern mismatch causes latency, reliability, and cost problems.

qs.q: An enterprise deployment requires Claude responses to be available offline or when the API is unreachable. What architecture handles this?
opts: This is impossible — Claude requires an API connection

A degraded-mode fallback: cache recent Claude outputs, serve cached responses for common queries, queue new requests for processing when connectivity returns, and display a clear indicator that responses may be cached
Use a local model as the primary and Claude as backup
Deploy Claude in the enterprise's own data center
qs.ex: Graceful degradation with caching is the production pattern for API dependency. Cache Claude's outputs for common queries, queue new requests during outages, and be transparent with users about cached vs. fresh responses.

qs.q: What is the purpose of a 'Claude gateway' in enterprise architecture?
opts: A physical network device that routes API traffic

A centralized service that sits between all internal Claude callers and the Anthropic API — handling authentication, rate limiting, cost allocation by team, prompt logging, and policy enforcement in one place
A content delivery network for Claude responses
A backup Claude deployment for high availability
qs.ex: A Claude gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns: one auth layer, shared rate limit management, per-team cost metering, centralized prompt/response logging, and policy enforcement. Without it, every team implements these differently (or not at all).

qs.q: A large enterprise client requires that all Claude requests and responses be logged for compliance. What architecture consideration does this create?
opts: Log everything to a text file on the application server

Implement a structured logging pipeline: async log shipping (not in the hot path), PII redaction before storage, tamper-evident storage (WORM or audit trail), defined retention policy, and access controls matching the sensitivity of the logged conversations
Logging is not possible with the Claude API
Only log error responses
qs.ex: Compliance logging has five requirements: async (latency impact), PII-redacted (data privacy), tamper-evident (audit integrity), retention-governed (legal hold vs. deletion), and access-controlled (least privilege). Missing any one of these creates compliance exposure.

qs.q: What is the enterprise-appropriate strategy for managing Claude API costs across 20 different internal teams?
opts: One shared API key for all teams — simplest to manage
Per-team API keys with budgets set in the Claude gateway; automatic alerts at 80% of budget and hard stops at 100%; monthly reporting to team leads — cost visibility drives responsible usage
Ask teams to self-report their usage monthly
Use the cheapest model for all teams to control costs
qs.ex: Per-team cost management: separate keys (or gateway routing keys) enable per-team metering. Budget alerts and hard stops prevent runaway costs. Monthly reporting creates accountability. This is standard FinOps applied to LLM API usage.

qs.q: What is 'input screening' in a Claude safety stack, and what does it catch?
opts: Spell-checking user input before sending to Claude

Checking that inputs are under the token limit
Rate limiting to prevent API abuse

Compressing Claude's output to save bandwidth
Translating Claude's output to the user's language

The system requires human approval for every request
Safety controls must be written in a compiled language

Logging which tools Claude calls

In the output only — catch and block any response containing investment advice

qs.q: A production Claude system's quality has silently degraded over 6 weeks due to prompt drift. What governance mechanism would have caught this?

Annual audit by external consultants

Mandatory adoption with usage tracking
Optional — let engineers choose whether to use it

A mandatory 8-hour training course
Just the API key

qs.q: A team wants to share Claude Code insights and best practices across the organization. What is the most scalable mechanism?

Mandatory quarterly training sessions
A dedicated internal Claude Code team that does all AI-assisted work

qs.q: How should a team handle a Claude Code-suggested code change that passes tests but the reviewer doesn't understand?

Reject it automatically — Claude Code outputs shouldn't be accepted without understanding
The reviewing engineer should ask Claude Code to explain its reasoning before accepting: 'Why did you make this change? What alternatives did you consider?' Understanding precedes approval
Escalate to a senior engineer to decide
qs.ex: The 'explain before accept' practice preserves engineering judgment. A change the reviewer doesn't understand cannot be maintained, debugged, or extended by the team. Claude Code should be able to explain its reasoning — and if it can't explain it clearly, that's a signal to reconsider.

qs.q: What is the operational impact of a poorly written CLAUDE.md on a 20-person engineering team?

Minor inconsistencies in style

Systematic inconsistency: every engineer's Claude Code session produces different conventions, test patterns, and architectural approaches — creating a codebase where each section reflects whoever wrote it rather than shared team standards
Claude Code stops working

Lines of code written per day
Claude API cost per PR

Split queries across 6 parallel Claude calls
Tell users the system cannot handle large document sets

qs.q: What is 'latency budget' in a production Claude system design?

The total time available for an end-user interaction (e.g. 3 seconds) allocated across each system component: API gateway (50ms), retrieval (200ms), Claude inference (2000ms), response post-processing (100ms), network (100ms) — every component gets a share of the total budget
The time Claude has to think before responding
The timeout setting on the HTTP client

A code review of the Claude integration
A comparison against competitor AI systems

Never allow the agent to take more than one action
Use human approval for every action

A statement that Claude is GDPR compliant
Anthropic's security certifications

Deploy one Claude instance per user

The number of tokens Claude can process per second
A billing metric unrelated to system design

Either — they are interchangeable
Agent — workflows cannot handle file processing

Have Claude generate engagement letters from scratch with no template

The first tool Claude will call
The model chosen for the task

qs.q: An enterprise client requires all Claude outputs to go through their legal team's review before being sent to customers. What integration pattern supports this?

Deploying Claude on two cloud providers for redundancy
Running blue for enterprise customers and green for consumers

qs.q: What is the purpose of a 'dead letter queue' in a Claude async processing pipeline?

A queue for low-priority batch requests
A backup queue used when the main queue is full

qs.q: A Claude system deployed for consumer-facing content generation begins showing signs of 'prompt injection via user content' in monitoring logs. What is the immediate and long-term response?

Ignore it — Claude is resistant to prompt injection

qs.q: What does 'grounding' mean in the context of a Claude production system's safety stack, and why does it matter?

Anchoring Claude's responses to provided source documents rather than pre-training knowledge — a grounded response can be traced to a specific document and verified; an ungrounded response relies on potentially outdated or hallucinated knowledge
A technique for reducing Claude's verbosity
Setting Claude's context to a specific geographic region
qs.ex: Grounding is a factual reliability control. A grounded RAG response is traceable: the claim appears in document X, section Y. An ungrounded response from pre-training cannot be verified and may be wrong or outdated. For regulated domains and high-stakes decisions, grounding is a mandatory architectural element.

qs.q: What is the difference between 'safety by design' and 'safety by policy' in Claude system architecture?

Safety by design is for consumer products; safety by policy is for enterprise
Safety by policy is more reliable because it uses Claude's training
qs.ex: Safety by design is technically enforced — a screener blocks prohibited content regardless of how Claude behaves. Safety by policy is instructional — it asks Claude to comply with rules, which it usually does but is not guaranteed. Production systems need both: design for the controls that must hold, policy for the behaviors that guide.

qs.q: A business stakeholder insists on a 99.999% uptime SLA for a Claude-powered feature. How should the architect respond?
opts: Agree — uptime SLAs are always achievable with good engineering
Commit to 99.999% uptime

Explain that Claude API SLAs (Anthropic's own) are 99.9% for the API itself; your application's uptime is bounded by Claude's API uptime. Propose: (1) a realistic SLA based on actual dependencies, (2) a graceful degradation design (cached responses when Claude is unavailable), and (3) transparent communication about the dependency
Route around Anthropic by running a local model
qs.ex: Professional SLA response: be honest about upstream dependencies, propose a realistic SLA based on actual data, design graceful degradation as the availability backstop, and communicate transparently. Overpromising on SLAs you cannot control is a professional and contractual risk.

qs.q: During discovery with a legal department, you learn that all AI-generated outputs must maintain a complete audit trail. What architectural elements satisfy this requirement?
opts: Store only the final outputs

Request/response logging (input prompt, model version, output, timestamp, user ID), immutable log storage, access controls on the log store, defined retention period matching legal hold requirements, and a query interface for auditors — the trail must be complete and tamper-evident
Enable verbose mode in Claude
Screenshot every Claude response
qs.ex: Audit trail for legal AI use has five elements: completeness (log everything — inputs and outputs), immutability (logs cannot be altered after the fact), access control (only authorized auditors can read), retention (match the legal hold period), and queryability (auditors can efficiently find specific interactions). Missing any one element fails audit requirements.

qs.q: A client's engineering team is skeptical about adopting Claude for a business-critical workflow. What is the architect's most effective approach?
opts: Override their skepticism — Claude adoption is mandatory
Show them benchmark data from other companies

Run a time-boxed proof of concept on a real but lower-risk version of their workflow, with agreed success metrics defined before starting — results from their own data with their own success criteria are more persuasive than external benchmarks
Build the full system and present it as a fait accompli
qs.ex: PoC-first with pre-agreed metrics is the trust-building approach. The team's skepticism is data: they need to see results with their own problem and their own success criteria, not external benchmarks. A time-boxed PoC with clear go/no-go criteria manages risk and builds credibility.

qs.q: A team has deployed a Claude system to production. What ongoing operational practices prevent quality drift over the next 12 months?
opts: Review the system prompt annually
No ongoing practices are needed — Claude's quality is stable

Weekly automated regression runs against the golden set, monthly review of flagged outputs from production monitoring, quarterly review of the golden set itself (add new patterns, retire obsolete ones), and a defined process for triaging and acting on quality alerts
Retrain Claude quarterly on new data
qs.ex: Quality maintenance is continuous: automated regression catches prompt/model changes that degrade quality; production monitoring surfaces real failures; golden set review keeps the eval current as the business evolves. Without these practices, quality drift goes undetected until users complain.

qs.q: What is a 'Claude system runbook' and who is its primary audience?
opts: Anthropic's internal documentation
Marketing material explaining Claude to potential users

An operational document for the team that maintains the system: what each alert means, how to diagnose it, how to respond, who to escalate to, how to roll back a prompt change, how to process a DSAR, how to handle a policy violation report — written for on-call engineers, not architects
Technical documentation for the compliance team only
qs.ex: A runbook is operational documentation for the team maintaining the live system. It answers the on-call engineer's question: 'This alert fired at 2am — what do I do?' It must be actionable, specific, and maintained. Runbooks without regular updates become useless as the system evolves.

qs.q: When should you recommend a 'human-in-the-loop' design over a fully autonomous Claude system to a client?
opts: Always — autonomous Claude systems are never appropriate

When the consequences of an error are high (financial loss, legal exposure, reputational damage, safety risk), when the client has not yet established a quality baseline for the system, or when regulatory requirements mandate human review — expand automation only after establishing measured trust
Only when the client is not comfortable with AI
When the task is too complex for Claude to handle alone
qs.ex: HITL vs. autonomous is a risk calibration decision. High consequence + unproven system = HITL is mandatory. Low consequence + proven accuracy = automation is appropriate. Regulatory mandate = HITL regardless of accuracy. The path from HITL to automation runs through measured performance data.

qs.q: A Claude system for a healthcare client must comply with HIPAA. What are the four technical safeguard areas the architect must address?
opts: Only encryption is required for HIPAA

Access controls (who can query the Claude system and see PHI in responses), audit controls (logging every access to PHI for 6 years), integrity controls (ensuring PHI in context is not altered), and transmission security (TLS for all data in transit) — all four are required HIPAA Technical Safeguard categories
HIPAA does not apply to AI systems
HIPAA compliance only requires a BAA with Anthropic
qs.ex: HIPAA Technical Safeguards have four categories. A BAA with Anthropic is also required but is not sufficient alone — your system must implement access controls, audit logging, integrity checking, and transmission encryption. The BAA covers Anthropic's handling; your architecture covers the application's handling.

qs.q: An enterprise wants to use Claude to generate SQL queries against their production database from natural language questions. What is the critical security design requirement?
opts: Let Claude generate and execute SQL directly — Claude's output is safe

Never execute Claude-generated SQL directly. Design a query validation layer that parses Claude's SQL, checks it against an allowlist of permitted tables and operations, parameterizes values, and requires read-only database credentials — Claude generates intent, your code makes it safe
Use a read-only user account and trust Claude's output
Only allow Claude to generate SELECT statements
qs.ex: LLM-to-database is a SQL injection risk. The validation layer is mandatory: parse the generated SQL, enforce table/operation allowlists, parameterize all values, and use minimal-privilege credentials. Read-only credentials help but are not sufficient if Claude generates queries that exfiltrate sensitive data from permitted tables.

qs.q: What is the purpose of a 'model risk management' framework for a bank deploying Claude in credit decisioning support?
opts: A framework for selecting which Claude model to use

A regulatory requirement (SR 11-7 for US banks) that mandates: documented model purpose and limitations, validation testing by a team independent of development, ongoing monitoring against defined performance thresholds, and approval by the model risk committee — required before any model is used in credit decisions
A cost management framework for Claude API usage
A framework for training bank employees on Claude
qs.ex: SR 11-7 model risk management applies to all models used in banking decisions, including AI/LLM-based systems. Banks must: document the model, validate it independently, monitor it continuously, and get committee approval. Architects must design the system to produce the documentation and monitoring artifacts this framework requires.
